title: Operators
overview: Operators are the tools Python uses to compute, compare, and combine. In this lecture you'll master arithmetic, comparison, and logical operators — the foundation of every decision and calculation in your programs.

blocks.content: At its core, a computer is a very fast calculator. Arithmetic operators tell Python to perform mathematical operations on numbers.
Python supports the operations you already know from maths — plus a few extra ones that are surprisingly useful.
`+` Addition · `-` Subtraction · `*` Multiplication · `/` Division · `//` Floor Division · `%` Modulus · `**` Exponentiation

blocks.title: Try It — All Arithmetic Operators
blocks.code:
a = 17
b = 5

print(a + b)   # 22
print(a - b)   # 12
print(a * b)   # 85
print(a / b)   # 3.4 (always float)
print(a // b)  # 3 (floor: drops decimal)
print(a % b)   # 2 (remainder)
print(a ** b)  # 1419857 (17 to the power 5)

blocks.content:
The two you might not know:

**Floor division `//`** — divides and discards the decimal. `17 // 5 = 3` not 3.4.

**Modulus `%`** — gives the **remainder** after division. `17 % 5 = 2` because 5 × 3 = 15, and 17 − 15 = 2.
Modulus is more useful than it sounds. `number % 2 == 0` tells you if a number is even. `seconds % 60` converts seconds to remaining seconds after full minutes.

analogy.title: Pizza Sharing
analogy.description: You have 17 slices and 5 friends. Floor division tells you how many slices each gets (3). Modulus tells you how many slices are left over (2). Both are real answers to a real problem.
bullets: You divide 17 slices equally among 5 friends.
Floor division tells you how many whole slices each person gets.
The modulus tells you how many slices are left over.
analogy.highlightCard: // gives whole slices, % gives the remainder — two sides of the same division.

bullets: // is floor division — it drops the decimal and gives the whole number.
% is the modulus — it gives the remainder after division.
Together they answer: 'how many each?' and 'how many left over?'
visualization.highlightCard: 17 // 5 = 3 (each gets 3 slices) and 17 % 5 = 2 (2 slices left over).

code.code:
slices = 17
friends = 5
print("Each gets:", slices // friends)
print("Left over:", slices % friends)
highlights: // divides and drops the decimal — the result is always a whole number.
% gives you the remainder after dividing as many times as possible.
Both operators work with any numbers, not just positive integers.
code.highlightCard: // and % are perfect partners — they split any division into quotient and remainder.

reflection.question: What does 10 % 3 evaluate to?
reflection.answer: 1 — because 3 × 3 = 9, and 10 − 9 = 1. The modulus is the remainder after division.

blocks.stage1Transition: Python has exactly these two division operators. Let's see how they work.
blocks.stage2Transition: Here is how // and % look in Python code.
blocks.takeaway: Dividing pizza teaches you Python's two division operators: // gives the whole result and % gives the remainder. Together they solve any division problem completely.

blocks.content: Arithmetic operators compute values. Comparison operators **compare** two values and always return `True` or `False`.
These are the questions your program asks before making a decision.
`==` Equal to · `!=` Not equal to · `>` Greater than · `<` Less than · `>=` Greater than or equal · `<=` Less than or equal

blocks.title: Try It — Comparison Operators
blocks.code:
marks = 75
passing_marks = 50

print(marks > passing_marks)   # True
print(marks == 100)            # False
print(marks != 75)             # False
print(marks >= passing_marks)  # True
print(marks < 50)              # False

blocks.content: **Common mistake:** `=` assigns a value. `==` compares two values. These are completely different. Never use `=` when you mean to compare.

analogy.title: Weighing Scale
analogy.description: A weighing scale compares two sides and tells you which is heavier, or if they're equal. Comparison operators do the same — compare two values and return True or False.
bullets: Place objects on both sides — the scale compares them instantly.
It tells you which side is heavier, or if they balance perfectly.
The answer is always one of three states: left heavy, right heavy, or equal.
analogy.highlightCard: Comparison operators compare two values and return either True or False.

visualization.title: a > b?
bullets: > checks if the left side is greater than the right.
< checks if the left side is smaller.
== checks if both sides are exactly equal — note: double equals sign.
visualization.highlightCard: Every comparison in Python produces exactly one result: True or False.

highlights: == is comparison (is it equal?), = is assignment (set it equal).
>, <, >=, <=, == and != are Python's six comparison operators.
Comparison results (True/False) can be stored in variables or used in conditions.
code.highlightCard: Comparison operators are the foundation of every decision your program makes.

reflection.question: What is the difference between = and == in Python?
reflection.answer: = assigns a value to a variable. == compares two values and returns True or False.

blocks.stage1Transition: Python does the same thing — it compares two values and gives you True or False.
blocks.stage2Transition: Here is how Python's comparison operators look in code.
blocks.takeaway: Comparison operators work like a weighing scale — they compare two values and return True or False. This True/False result is what drives every if-statement in your program.

blocks.title: Exam Result Check
blocks.instructions: A student scored 68 marks. The passing mark is 40 and the distinction mark is 75. Write code to check and print: Is the student passing? (>=40) Is the student getting distinction? (>=75)
blocks.starterCode:
score = 68
passing = 40
distinction = 75

# Check and print results
print("Passed:", )
print("Distinction:", )
blocks.solution:
score = 68
passing = 40
distinction = 75

print("Passed:", score >= passing)
print("Distinction:", score >= distinction)
blocks.hint: Use >= to check if score meets or exceeds the threshold.

blocks.content: Comparison operators answer one question at a time. But real decisions often need multiple conditions checked at once.
Logical operators let you **combine** comparisons into compound conditions.

**`and`** — both conditions must be True.

**`or`** — at least one condition must be True.

**`not`** — reverses a condition (True becomes False, False becomes True).

blocks.title: Try It — Logical Operators
blocks.code:
age = 20
has_id = True

# and: both must be true
print(age >= 18 and has_id)    # True

# or: at least one true
print(age < 18 or has_id)      # True

# not: reverse
print(not has_id)               # False

blocks.title: Try It — Real Scenario
blocks.code:
marks = 72
attendance = 80

# Student passes if marks >= 50 AND attendance >= 75
passes = marks >= 50 and attendance >= 75
print("Eligible for exam:", passes)

# Student gets scholarship if marks > 90 OR attendance == 100
scholarship = marks > 90 or attendance == 100
print("Scholarship eligible:", scholarship)
blocks.expectedOutput:
Eligible for exam: True
Scholarship eligible: False

analogy.title: College Entry Rules
analogy.description: To enter the college library: you need a valid ID card AND you must be a registered student. Both must be true. That's 'and'. To access the WiFi: you can use your student email OR your roll number. Either one works. That's 'or'.
bullets: Library access: you need a valid ID AND be a registered student — both must be true.
WiFi access: use your student email OR your roll number — either one works.
Two completely different logic systems for two different situations.
analogy.highlightCard: and requires both conditions to be true. or requires at least one to be true.

visualization.title: and vs or
bullets: and returns True only when BOTH conditions on either side are True.
or returns True when AT LEAST ONE condition is True.
not flips the result — True becomes False, and False becomes True.
visualization.highlightCard: and = both must pass. or = either can pass. not = flip the result.

code.code:
has_card = True
is_registered = True
print("Library access:", has_card and is_registered)
highlights: and checks both conditions — if either is False, the whole thing is False.
or checks both conditions — if either is True, the whole thing is True.
Combine multiple conditions to express complex real-world rules in code.
code.highlightCard: Logical operators let you combine conditions to express any real-world rule in Python.

reflection.question: True and False evaluates to?
reflection.answer: False — because 'and' requires BOTH sides to be True. Since one side is False, the result is False.

blocks.stage1Transition: Python has 'and' and 'or' operators that work exactly the same way. Let's see.
blocks.stage2Transition: Here is how and, or, and not look in Python code.
blocks.takeaway: Logical operators (and, or, not) work like real-world rules — and requires everything, or accepts anything, not flips the answer. Use them to combine conditions in your programs.

keyTakeaways.text: +, -, *, / are basic arithmetic. // gives the floor (no decimal), % gives the remainder.
Modulus (%) is great for checking even/odd or finding remainders.
Comparison operators (==, !=, >, <, >=, <=) always return True or False.
= assigns. == compares. Never mix them up.
and: both conditions must be True. or: at least one must be True. not: reverses the result.
Logical operators let you combine multiple conditions into one expression.

whatYouLearned: All seven arithmetic operators including floor division and modulus
All six comparison operators and what they return
The three logical operators: and, or, not
How to combine conditions for real-world decision making

quiz.question: What is the result of 15 % 4?
quiz.explanation: Modulus gives the remainder after division. 4 × 3 = 12, and 15 − 12 = 3. So 15 % 4 = 3.

quiz.question: What does 10 // 3 return?
quiz.explanation: Floor division (//) divides and drops the decimal part. 10 ÷ 3 = 3.33, but // gives just 3.

quiz.question: True and False evaluates to?
quiz.explanation: The 'and' operator returns True only when BOTH sides are True. Since one side is False, the result is False.

quiz.question: Which statement correctly checks if a number is even?
quiz.explanation: A number is even if its remainder when divided by 2 is 0. The modulus operator (%) gives the remainder, so number % 2 == 0 correctly checks for even numbers.

quiz.question: What is the value of: not (5 > 3)?
quiz.explanation: 5 > 3 is True. The 'not' operator reverses it, so not True = False.

quiz.question: What does 2 ** 8 evaluate to?
quiz.explanation: The ** operator is exponentiation. 2 ** 8 means 2 to the power of 8 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 256.

problems.title: Simple Calculator
problems.description:
Write a program that takes two numbers as input and prints the result of all 5 operations: addition, subtraction, multiplication, floor division, and modulus.

Example (a=10, b=3):
10 + 3 = 13
10 - 3 = 7
10 * 3 = 30
10 // 3 = 3
10 % 3 = 1
problems.starterCode:
a = int(input("Enter first number: "))
b = int(input("Enter second number: "))

# Print all 5 operations
problems.solution:
a = int(input("Enter first number: "))
b = int(input("Enter second number: "))

print(f"{a} + {b} = {a + b}")
print(f"{a} - {b} = {a - b}")
print(f"{a} * {b} = {a * b}")
print(f"{a} // {b} = {a // b}")
print(f"{a} % {b} = {a % b}")

problems.title: Time Converter
problems.description:
Ask the user for a total number of seconds. Convert and print it as hours, minutes, and remaining seconds.

Example (7384 seconds):
Hours: 2
Minutes: 3
Seconds: 4

Hint: hours = seconds // 3600, remaining = seconds % 3600, minutes = remaining // 60
problems.starterCode:
total_seconds = int(input("Enter total seconds: "))

# Convert to hours, minutes, seconds
problems.solution:
total_seconds = int(input("Enter total seconds: "))

hours = total_seconds // 3600
remaining = total_seconds % 3600
minutes = remaining // 60
seconds = remaining % 60

print(f"Hours: {hours}")
print(f"Minutes: {minutes}")
print(f"Seconds: {seconds}")
